{{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, xxv.}}}}

¶
'''whilesas†''', ''conj.'' [< ''whiles'' + ''as''<sup>1</sup>.] Same as ''whileas.'' [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Whose noble acts renownèd were
''Whilesas'' he livèd everywhere.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Fame’s Memorial, Epitaphs.}}}}

'''whilk'''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'' Another form of ''whelk''<sup>2</sup>, properly ''welk, wilk.''

'''whilk'''<sup>2</sup> (hwilk), ''pron.'' and ''a.'' An obsolete or Scotch form of ''which''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|“What, ''whilk'' way is he geen?” he gan to crie.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Reeve’s Tale, l. 158.}}}}

'''whilk'''<sup>3</sup> (hwilk), ''n.'' The scoter, ''Œdemia nigra. Montagu.'' See cut under ''scoter.'' [Local, Brit.]

'''whilly''' (hwil′i), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''whillied'', ppr. ''whillying.'' [A dial. form, perhaps a mixture of ''wile''<sup>1</sup> with ''wheedle.''] To cajole by wheedling; whilly-wha. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|These baptized idols of theirs brought pike-staves and sandalled shoon from all the four winds, and ''whillied'' the old women out of their corn and their candle-ends.
{{right|''Scott'', Abbot, xvi.}}}}

'''whilly-wha, whilly-whaw''' (hwil′i-hwâ), ''v.'' [Appar. a mere extension of ''whilly.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To use cajolery or make wheedling speeches. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|What, man! the life of a King, and many thousands besides, is not to be weighed with the chance of two young things ''whilly-whawing'' in ilk other’s ears for a minute.
{{right|''Scott'', Quentin Durward, xxxi.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To cajole; wheedle; delude with specious pretenses. [Scotch.]

raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|whiggery|6899|whilom}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|I’ll hae nae ''whiggery'' in the barony of Tillietudlem — the next thing wad be to set up a conventicle in my very withdrawing room.
{{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, vii.}}}}

{{smaller block|Our friend was a hearty toper in the days of his ''Whiggery'', but no sooner turned one of the tautest of Tories than he took to the teapot. It seems a thing against nature.
{{right|''Noctes Ambrosianæ'', Sept., 1832.}}}}

'''whiggification''' (hwig″i-fi-kā′shon), ''n.''   [< ''whig''<sup>3</sup> + ''-i-fication''.]   A making or becoming whiggish. [Humorous.]
{{smaller block|We were all along against the ''whiggification'' of the Tory System.
{{right|''Noctes Ambrosianæ'', Sept., 1832.}}}}

'''whiggish''' (hwig′ish), ''a.''   [< ''whig''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]   Of or pertaining to whigs, in any application of the name; partaking of the principles of whigs.
{{smaller block|To the shame and grief of every ''whiggish'', loyal, and true Protestant heart.
{{right|''Swift'', Polite Conversation, Int.}}}}

'''whiggishly''' (hwig′ish-li), ''adv.'' In a whiggish manner.
{{smaller block|Being ''whiggishly'' inclined, [Thomas Cox] was deprived of that Office in Oct., 1683.
{{right|''Wood'', Fasti Oxon., II. 54.}}}}

'''whiggishness''' (hwig′ish-nes), ''n.'' The character of being whiggish; whiggery.
{{smaller block|Mr. Walpole has himself that trait of ''Whiggishness'' which peculiarly fits him to paint the portrait of the chief of the Whigs.
{{right|''The Academy'', Nov. 16, 1889, p. 311.}}}}

'''whiggism''' (hwig′izm), ''n.''   [< ''whig''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ism''.]   The principles of the whigs; whiggery.
{{smaller block|As if ''whiggism'' were an admirable cordial in the mass, though the several ingredients are rank poisons.
{{right|''Dryden'', Vind. of Duke of Guise.}}}}

'''whigling''' (hwig′ling), ''n.''   [< ''whig''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.]   A whig, in any sense: used in contempt.   ''Spectator.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')

'''whigmaleerie, whigmeleerie''' (hwig-mạ-, hwig-mẹ-lē′ri), ''n.''   [Also ''whigmaleery;'' origin obscure; appar. a fantastic name.]   Any fantastical ornament; a trinket; a knickknack; also, a whim or crotchet. Also used attributively. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Some fewer ''whigmaleeries'' in your noddle.
{{right|''Burns,'' Brigs of Ayr.}}}}
{{smaller block|Ah! it’s a brave kirk — nane o’ yere ''whigmaleeries'' and curliewurlies and open-steek hems about it — a’ solid, weel-jointed mason-wark. {{right|''Scott,'' Rob Roy, xix.}}}}
{{smaller block|I met ane very honest, fair-spoken, weel-put-on gentleman, . . . that was in the ''whigmaleery'' man’s [silversmith’s] back shop. {{right|''Scott,'' Fortunes of Nigel, iii.}}}}

'''whigship''' (hwig′ship), ''n.''   [< ''whig''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ship.'']   Whiggism. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|People of your cast in politics are fond of vilifying our country. Is this your ''Whigship?''
{{right|''Landor,'' Imag. Conv., Johnson and John Horne (Tooke), i.}}}}

'''while'''<sup>1</sup> (hwīl), ''n.''   [< ME. ''while, whil, whyle, qvile, wile, hwile,'' < AS. ''hwīl,'' a time, = OS. ''hwīla'' = OFries. ''hwile, wile'' = D. ''wijl'' = LG. ''wile'' = OHG. ''wīla,'' MHG. ''wīle,'' G. ''weile,'' time, period or point of time, hour, = Icel. ''hvīla,'' place of rest, bed, = Sw. ''hvila'' = Dan. ''hvile,'' rest, = Goth. ''hweila,'' a time, season; perhaps akin to OBulg. ''po-chiti,'' rest, L. ''quies,'' rest: see ''quiet.'']   '''1.''' A time; a space of time; especially, a short space of time during which something happens or is to happen or be done.
<poem>Many a tyme he layd hym downe,
And shot another ''whyle.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Lytell Geste of Robyn Hode'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 98).}}}}

{{smaller block|Yes, signior, thou art even he we speak of all this ''while.''
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Love’s Cure, ii. 1.}}}}

<poem>In the primeval age a dateless ''while''
The vacant Shepherd wander’d with his flock.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Coleridge'', Religious Musings.}}}}

'''2.''' Time spent upon anything; expenditure of time, and hence of pains or labor; trouble: as, to do it is not worth one’s ''while.''

<poem>A clerk hadde litherly biset [evilly spent] his ''whyle'',
But if he koude a carpenter bigyle.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 113.}}}}

<poem>If Jelousie doth thee payne,
Quyte hym his ''while'' thus agayne.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 4392.}}}}

<poem>Woe the ''while''
That brought such wanderer to our isle!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., ii. 15.}}}}

<poem>What Cambridge saw not strikes us yet
As scarcely worth one’s ''while'' to see.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Lowell'', To Holmes.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Alas the while.''' See ''alas.''—'''Every once in a while.''' See ''every''<sup>1</sup>.—'''In the mean while.''' See ''mean''<sup>3</sup>, 3.—'''The while, the whiles†''', during the time something else is going on; in the mean time: from this expression the conjunctive use is derived.}}

<poem>Do the body speke so
Right as hit woned was to do,
''The whyles'' that it was on lyve?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Death of Blanche, l. 151.}}}}

<poem>''The whiles'', with hollow throates,
The Choristers the joyous Antheme sing.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Spenser'', Epithalamion, l. 220.}}}}

<poem>If you’ll sit down,
I’ll bear your logs ''the while.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iii. 1. 24.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Worth while''', worth the time which it requires; worth the time and pains; worth the trouble and expense. See def. 2, above.}}
{{smaller block|What fate has disposed of the papers, ’tis not ''worth while'' to tell.
{{right|''Locke.''}}}}
{{smaller block|How! don’t you think it ''worth while'' to agree in the lie?
{{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, iv. 3.}}}}

'''while<sup>1</sup>''' (hwīl), ''conj.'' and ''adv.''   [< ME. ''while'', ''whil'', ''whyl'', ''hwile'', etc. (= MHG. ''wīle'', G. ''weil'', because); abbr. of the orig. phrase ''the while that'', < AS. ''thā hwīle the'' (MHG. ''die wīle'', G. ''die weil''), ‘the while that,’ where ''hwīle'' is acc. of ''hwīl'', while, time (other constructions also being used; cf. D. ''terwijl'', G. ''derweil'', while, orig. genitive): see ''while'', ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''conj.'' '''1.''' During or in the time that; as long as.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Whil'' I have tyme and space, . . .
Me thynketh it acordaunt to resoun
To telle yow. ''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 35.</poem>
<poem>''While'' that the armed hand doth fight abroad,
The advised head defends itself at home.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., i. 2. 178.}}}}
{{smaller block|''While'' you were catering for Mirabell I have been Broaker for you.
{{right|''Congreve'', Way of the World, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''While'' stands the Coliseum, Rome shall stand.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv. 145.}}}}
'''2.''' At the same time that: often used adversatively.
{{smaller block|<poem>He wonder’d that your lordship
Would suffer him to spend his youth at home,
''While'' other men, of slender reputation,
Put forth their sons to seek preferment out.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., i. 3. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|''While'' we condemn the politics, we cannot but respect the principles, of the man.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 25.}}}}
'''3.''' Till; until. [Now prov. Eng. and U. S.]

<poem>We will keep ourself
Till supper-time alone; ''while'' then, God be with you!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 1. 44.}}}}
<poem>A younger brother, but in some disgrace
Now with my friends; and want some little means
To keep me upright, ''while'' things be reconciled.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''B. Jonson'', Devil is an Ass, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|At Maltby there lived, some years ago, a retired druggist. The boys’ Sunday-school was confided to his management, and he had a way of appealing to them when they were disorderly which is still quoted by those who often heard it: “Now, boys, I can’t do nothing ''while'' you are quiet.”
{{right|''J. Earle.''}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn. 2.''' ''While, Though.'' ''While'' implies less of contrast in the parallel than ''though'', sometimes, indeed, implying no contrast at all. Thus we say, “''While'' I admire his bravery, I esteem his moderation;” but “''though'' I admire his courage, I detest his cruelty.”}}

'''II.†''' ''adv.'' At times; sometimes; now and then: used in correlation as ''while . . . while.'' Compare ''whiles, adv.''

{{smaller block|Godes wrake cumeth on this woreld to wrekende on sunfulle men here gultes, . . . binimeth hem ''hwile'' oref [cattle], . . . ''hwile'' here hele [health], & ''hwile'' here ogen [own] lif.
{{right|''Rel. Antiq.'', I. 128.}}}}

'''while<sup>2</sup>''' (hwīl), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''whiled'', ppr. ''whiling''.   [< ME. *''hwilen'', in comp. ''ihwilen'' = OHG. ''wīlōn'', MHG. ''wīlen'', sojourn, stay, rest, G. ''weilen'', linger, loiter, stay, = Icel. ''hvíla'' = Sw. ''hvila'' = Dan. ''hvile'', rest, = Goth. ''hweilan'', pause a while, cease; from the noun, in the orig. sense as in Goth. ''hweila'', pause, rest: see ''while''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cause to pass; spend; consume; kill: said of time: usually followed by ''away''.

<poem>Nor do I beg this slender inch, to ''while''
The time ''away''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, iii. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And all the day
The weaver plies his shuttle, and ''whiles away''
The peaceful hours with songs of battles past.</poem>
{{right|''R. H. Stoddard'', History.}}}}
'''2†.''' To occupy the time of; busy; detain.
{{smaller block|Still lakes, thicke woods, and varietie of Continent-obseruations haue thus long ''whiled'' vs.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 705.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To pass; elapse, as time. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|They . . . must necessarily fly to new acquisitions of beauty to pass away the ''whiling'' moments and intervals of life: for with them every hour is heavy that is not joyful. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 522.}}}}

'''whileas†''', ''conj.''   [< ''while''<sup>1</sup> + ''as''<sup>1</sup>.]   While.
{{smaller block|<poem>But Burn cannot his grief asswage, ''whileas'' his dayes endureth,
To see the Changes of this Age, which day and time procureth.</poem>
''Nichol Burn'', in Roxburghe Ballads (ed. Ebsworth), VI. 608.}}

'''whilemeal†''', ''adv.''   [ME. ''whilmele''; < ''while''<sup>1</sup> + ''-meal'' as in ''piecemeal'', ''stoundmeal'', etc.]   By turns; by courses; at a time.
{{smaller block|He [Solomon] sente hem into the wode, ten thousand bi eche moneth ''whilmele'', so that two monethis ''whilmele'' thei weren in her howsis. {{right|''Wyclif'', 3 Ki. [1 Ki.] v. 14.}}}}

'''whilend†''', ''a.'' Passing; transient; transitory. Compare ''while''<sup>2</sup>, ''v. i.''
{{smaller block|For that ''hwilende'' lust [there is] endeles pine [pain].
{{right|''Hali Meidenhad'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 25.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>This world fareth ''hwilynde'',
Hwenne on cumeth other goth.</poem>
{{right|''Old Eng. Misc.'' (ed. Morris), p. 94.}}}}

'''whileness†''', ''n.''   [ME. ''whileness''; < ''while''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ness''.]   Time as vicissitude; transitoriness; change. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Anentis whom is not ouerchaunginge, nether schadewing of ''whileness'', or tyme [tr. L. ''vicissitudinis obumbratio''].
{{right|''Wyclif'', Jas. i. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thurgh oure might & oure monhod maintene to gedur!
What ''whylenes'', or wanspede, wryxles [overpowers] our
mynde? ''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 9327.</poem>}}

'''whilere†''' (hwīl-ãr′), ''adv.''   [Early mod. E. also ''whileare'', ''whyleare''; < ME. ''while er'', ''whill ere''; < ''while''<sup>1</sup> + ''ere''<sup>1</sup>.]   A little while ago; hitherto; some time ago; erewhile.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Whill ere'' thu bad I shuld reche the thy sheld,
And now me think thu hast nede of on,
ffor neyther spere ne sheld that thu may weld.</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2361.}}}}
{{smaller block|Whose learned Muse thou cherisht most ''whilere''.
{{right|''L. Bryskett'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 278).}}}}

'''whiles''' (hwīlz), ''conj.'' and ''adv.''   [< ME. ''whiles'', ''whyles'', ''qwylles'', etc., adverbial gen. of ''hwil'' (reg. gen. ''hwile''), while: see ''while''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''whilst''.]   '''I.†''' ''conj.'' While; during the time that; as long as; at the same time that.
{{smaller block|<poem>Withowttene changynge in chace, thies ware the cheefe
armes
Of Arthure the avenaunt, ''qwhylles'' he in erthe lengede.</poem>
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3652.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whiles'' they are weake, betimes with them contend.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. iv. 34.}}}}
{{smaller block|Agree with thine adversary quickly, ''whiles'' thou art in the way with him. {{right|Mat. v. 25.}}}}

'''II.''' ''adv.'' At times. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>I tuk his body on my back,
And ''whiles'' I gaed, and ''whiles'' I satt.</poem>
{{right|''The Lament of the Border Widow'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 87).}}}}
{{smaller block|Mony a time I hae helped Jenny Dennison out o’ the winnock, forbye creeping in ''whiles'' mysell.
{{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, xxv.}}}}

'''whilesas†''', ''conj.''   [< ''whiles'' + ''as''<sup>1</sup>.]   Same as ''whileas.'' [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Whose noble acts renownèd were
''Whilesas'' he livèd everywhere.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Fame’s Memorial, Epitaphs.}}}}

'''whilk'''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'' Another form of ''whelk''<sup>2</sup>, properly ''welk, wilk.''

'''whilk'''<sup>2</sup> (hwilk), ''pron.'' and ''a.'' An obsolete or Scotch form of ''which''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|“What, ''whilk'' way is he geen?” he gan to crie.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Reeve’s Tale, l. 158.}}}}

'''whilk'''<sup>3</sup> (hwilk), ''n.'' The scoter, ''Œdemia nigra. Montagu.'' See cut under ''scoter.'' [Local, Brit.]

'''whilly''' (hwil′i), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''whillied'', ppr. ''whillying.''   [A dial. form, perhaps a mixture of ''wile''<sup>1</sup> with ''wheedle.'']   To cajole by wheedling; whilly-wha. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|These baptized idols of theirs brought pike-staves and sandalled shoon from all the four winds, and ''whillied'' the old women out of their corn and their candle-ends.
{{right|''Scott'', Abbot, xvi.}}}}

'''whilly-wha, whilly-whaw''' (hwil′i-hwâ), ''v.''   [Appar. a mere extension of ''whilly.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To use cajolery or make wheedling speeches. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|What, man! the life of a King, and many thousands besides, is not to be weighed with the chance of two young things ''whilly-whawing'' in ilk other’s ears for a minute.
{{right|''Scott'', Quentin Durward, xxxi.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To cajole; wheedle; delude with specious pretenses. [Scotch.] {{smaller block|Wylie Mactrickit the writer . . . canna ''whilli-wha'' me as he ’s dune mony a ane. {{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, xl.}}}}

'''whilly-wha, whilly-whaw''' (hwil′i-hwâ), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [< ''whilly-wha, v.'']   '''I.''' ''n.'' A wheedling speech; cajolery.

{{smaller block|I wish ye binna beginning to learn the way of blawing in a woman’s lug, wi’ a’ your ''whilly-wha’s!''
{{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, v.}}}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Cajoling; wheedling; smooth-tongued. [Scotch.]

{{smaller block|Because he ’s a ''whilly-whaw'' body, and has a plausible tongue of his own, . . . they have made him Prövost!
{{right|''Scott'', Redgauntlet, xii.}}}}

'''whilom''' (hwī′lōm), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [Early mod. E. also ''whilome, whylome''; < ME. ''whilom, whilome, whylom, whilum, whilem, hwilem, whilen, hwilen, wilen,'' < AS. ''hwīlum,'' at times, sometimes (''hwīlum . . . hwīlum,'' now . . . then), dat. or instr. pl. of ''hwīl,'' time, point of time.]   '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' At times; by times.

<poem>Untenderly fro the toppe thai tiltine to-gederz;
''Whilome'' Arthure over, and other while undyre.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1145.}}</poem>

'''2.''' Once; formerly; once upon a time.

<poem>''Whylom,'' as olde stories tellen us,
Ther was a duk that highte Theseus.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1.}}</poem>

{{smaller block|Here is Trapezonde also, ''whilome'' bearing the proude name of an Empire. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 320.}}}}

<poem>For so Apollo, with unweeting hand,
''Whilom'' did slay his dearly loved mate.
{{right|''Milton'', Death of a Fair Infant.}}</poem><noinclude><references/></noinclude>
